## The question

[Local Max of an Integral](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1111208/local-max-of-an-integral), asked by [user3776749](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/181642/user3776749) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-01-19; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I'm having trouble with the following problem.
>
> > $f(x)=\int_0^x \frac{t^2-4}{1+cos^2(t)}dt$
> > 
> > At what value of $x$ does the local max of $f(x)$ occur?
>
> I've tried just taking the integral then finding the Max using critical points, but I can't find a way to make the integration straight forward using trig identities and algebra. So either I'm missing something on that front or there is another approach I'm not privy to.
:::

Hint: There is a theorem about differentiating functions of the form
$$f(x) = \int_0^x g(t) \,dt$$
It's a very important theorem.  Some may even call it fundamental.

<!---
By the first fundamental theorem of calculus
$$f'(x) = g(x)$$
So for your function
$$f'(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{1 + \cos^2 x}$$
The critical points are the zeroes of this function, apparently $\pm 2$.  Lucky for us the denominator is at least $1$, so we only need to look at the numerator to determine the sign of the derivative.  

At $x=-2$, $f'$ changes sign from positive to negative, making this point a local maximum.  At $x=+2$, $f'$ changes from negative to positive, making this point a local minimum.  
-->
